Partnership System Notes

The full explanation behind our convention card: what each bid means, when it applies, what comes next, worked examples and the usual traps. Base system 2/1 Game Forcing, 1NT 15–17, revised 11 Oct 2026.

← One-page Convention Card

How to use these notes

Tiers show how often each convention comes up. Learn them in order:

  • Tier 0 Core system. Comes up every session; know it cold.
  • Tier 1 Most sessions. Learn after Tier 0 feels automatic.
  • Tier 2 Occasional but valuable. Learn last.

Notation. An auction is written left to right in turn order, with the opponents' calls in brackets: 1♥–(2♣)–X means partner opened 1♥, right-hand opponent overcalled 2♣ and you doubled. A hand is written ♠KJ74 ♥83 ♦Q9752 ♣K6.

Abbreviation Meaning
M / m A major (♥ ♠) / a minor (♣ ♦)
X / XX / P Double / redouble / pass
HCP High-card points: A = 4, K = 3, Q = 2, J = 1
GF Game forcing: neither partner may pass below game
NF Non-forcing: partner may pass
Opener / responder The player who opened / that player's partner
Overcaller / advancer The opponent who bid first for their side / that player's partner

Counting your hand

  • Opening hands use HCP. Add a point for a good 5-card suit if you are close.
  • Raising partner's suit uses dummy points: HCP plus shortness.
Shortness With 4+ trumps With 3 trumps
Void +5 +3
Singleton +3 +2
Doubleton +1 +1
  • Honors in short suits lose value, so adjust before adding shortness:
Short holding Count the honor as Then add shortness?
Singleton A 4 (full) Yes
Singleton K 2 (1 less) Yes
Singleton Q or J 0 Yes
Doubleton AK, AQ, KQ, Ax, Kx Full Yes (+1)
Doubleton Qx, Jx, QJ 1 less (Qx = 1, Jx = 0, QJ = 2) Yes (+1)
  • Only count dummy points with a fit, and never for shortness in partner's own suit.
  • Game needs about 25 points between you (26 for 3NT is safer), small slam about 33, grand slam about 37.

Opening bids Tier 0

Requirements by seat

Seat Open a 1-level suit with
1st and 2nd 12+ HCP, or the Rule of 20: HCP + cards in your two longest suits ≥ 20
3rd Can be light, about 10 HCP, with a good suit you want partner to lead. Drury protects you
4th 14+ HCP: always open. 9–13 HCP: open only with the Rule of 15 (HCP + number of spades ≥ 15); otherwise pass the hand out. Never preempt

Rule of 20 example: ♠KQ1083 ♥AJ974 ♦5 ♣84 has 10 HCP + 5 + 5 = 20. Open 1♠ (the higher of two 5-card suits).

Rule of 15 example (4th seat): ♠KQ94 ♥A82 ♦Q73 ♣952 has 11 HCP + 4 spades = 15. Open 1♣. Without the spades, passing is safer because the opponents would win the fight for the part-score.

Choosing the suit

  1. 5-card major? Open it. With 5-5 in the majors, open 1♠.
  2. Balanced with 15–17? Open 1NT, even with a 5-card major (♠AK ♥KJ862 ♦Q74 ♣K93 = 16, open 1NT).
  3. Otherwise open a minor: - 1♦ promises 4+ diamonds. The single exception is 4♠ 4♥ 3♦ 2♣, which opens 1♦ with three. - 1♣ promises 3+ clubs. With 3-3 in the minors, open 1♣. - 4-4 in the minors, open 1♦. 5-5 in the minors, open 1♦.
  4. Two suits of different lengths: open the longer. With 6-5, open the 6-card suit and bid the other suit twice if the auction allows.

The full list

Opening Meaning
1♣ 3+ clubs, 12–21
1♦ 4+ diamonds (3 only with 4♠ 4♥ 3♦ 2♣), 12–21
1♥ / 1♠ 5+ cards, 12–21
1NT 15–17 balanced (4-3-3-3, 4-4-3-2, 5-3-3-2; an occasional 6-3-2-2 with a 6-card minor). Never with a singleton
2♣ Strong, artificial: 22+ balanced, or about 9 playing tricks
2♦ / 2♥ / 2♠ Weak two: 6-card suit, 5–10 HCP
2NT 20–21 balanced
3♣ – 3♠ Preempt: about 7 cards, weak
3NT Gambling: solid 7+ card minor (AKQxxxx) and no A or K outside
4♣ – 4♠ Preempt: about 8 cards, weak

2/1 Game Forcing Tier 0

The idea in one sentence

When partner opens 1♦, 1♥ or 1♠ and you answer with a new suit at the 2-level without jumping, you are promising an opening hand yourself (12+). From that moment both of you must keep bidding until you reach game.

"2/1" (say "two over one") means a 2-level bid over a 1-level opening.

Why it's worth learning

Two opening hands together (12 + 12 = 24+) are almost always worth game. 2/1 tells partner that on the first response, so for the rest of the auction:

  • No one has to jump to show strength. You can't be dropped below game, so you can bid slowly and naturally.
  • You get room to compare options. Spades or notrump? Game or slam? There are several bids left to find out.
  • Strength is shown by speed (see fast arrival below): slow means interested in more, a jump to game means "that's enough".

In older Standard American, 1♠–2♣ was forcing for one round only. Responder with 13 had to keep inventing forcing bids or jump around, which used up space. 2/1 solves that with one agreement.

Exactly which bids are 2/1?

Auction 2/1 game force? Why
1♠–2♣, 1♠–2♦, 1♠–2♥ Yes New suit at the 2-level, no jump
1♥–2♣, 1♥–2♦ Yes Same
1♦–2♣ Yes Same
1♥–2♠ No Jump (1♠ was available): weak jump shift
1♣–2♦ No Jump (1♦ was available): weak jump shift
1♣–2♣, 1♦–2♦ No A raise: inverted minor
1♠–2♠, 1♥–2♥ No A raise: 6–9
1♥–1♠, 1♦–1♥ No 1-level response: forcing one round, 6+
1♠–1NT No Forcing 1NT, 6–12
1♠–2NT No Jacoby 2NT (a different game force: 4+ trumps)

Not game forcing at the 1-level: 1♥–1♠ can be a 6-point hand, even though it's forcing for one round. If responder has 15 points with 4 spades, they still bid 1♠ and show the strength on their next bid.

What responder needs for a 2/1

Bid Strength Length
2♣ 12+ 4+ clubs usually. Can be 3 with a balanced game-forcing hand and nothing else to bid
2♦ 12+ 4+ diamonds (usually 5)
2♥ over 1♠ 12+ 5+ hearts

Count it like an opening hand: if you would have opened this hand yourself, you have enough for a 2/1.

Exactly 12: 2/1 or 1NT?

1NT is 6–12 and 2/1 is 12+, so 12 is a judgment call. 11 or less always bids 1NT; 13+ always makes a 2/1 (or a game-forcing raise). With exactly 12, look at the quality of the points:

Upgrade: treat as 13, bid 2/1 Downgrade: treat as 11, bid 1NT
A good 5+ card suit (2 of the top 3 honors) Flat 4-3-3-3 shape
Points in aces and kings Points in queens and jacks
Tens and nines with your honors (KJ109) Honors in short suits (Qx, singleton K)
3-card support for opener's major No fit and no good suit
Two-suited shape (5-4, 5-5)

A good 12 makes a 2/1. A bad 12 bids 1NT and then invites.

Choosing 1NT with a bad 12 costs very little: your second bid invites game (2NT, or 3M with 3-card support). Opener accepts with 13+, so you still reach game. You only stop below game when opener is also minimum, and then 12 + 12 with poor cards is better played in a part-score.

After 1♠, your hand HCP Verdict Bid
♠Q4 ♥A5 ♦KQJ1063 ♣974 12 Good: strong 6-card suit 2♦
♠Q4 ♥QJ5 ♦QJ73 ♣KJ62 12 Bad: flat, all queens and jacks 1NT, then 2NT (invite)
♠K73 ♥A84 ♦A962 ♣1074 11 + 3 trumps Aces, but only 11 1NT, then 3♠ (limit raise)
♠K73 ♥A84 ♦A962 ♣J74 12 + 3 trumps Good: two aces and a fit 2♦ (2/1), support spades next

Responder's plan after 1♠ (or 1♥)

Work down this list and stop at the first line that fits:

Your hand Bid
0–5 Pass
4+ spades The raise ladder: 2♠ (6–9), 3♠ (10–12), 2NT Jacoby (13+), splinter, 4♠ (weak, shapely)
3 spades, 6–9 2♠
3 spades, 10–12 1NT, then jump to 3♠ next time
3 spades, 12+ 2/1 in your best suit, then support spades on your next bid
No fit, 6–11 1NT (forcing)
No fit, 12+ 2/1 in your longest suit (2♥ needs 5; with only 4 hearts bid a minor first)
Over 1♥ with 4+ spades 1♠ at any strength, then show strength next

Two-suiter examples, after partner's 1♠:

  • ♠4 ♥KQ97 ♦A8 ♣KJ8642 (13). Bid 2♣: your long suit first. Show hearts later if useful.
  • ♠Q4 ♥AQ83 ♦K105 ♣Q942 (13, balanced, 4 hearts). Bid 2♣, not 2♥ (2♥ needs 5). Hearts can come later.
  • ♠K6 ♥Q842 ♦AJ5 ♣K107 (13, balanced). Bid 2♣ with only three clubs: 2♥ needs 5 cards and 2♦ needs 4.

Opener's second bid

After 1♠–2♣, game is forced. Opener just describes the hand; there's no need to show strength yet.

Opener rebids Meaning
2♦ / 2♥ Natural, 4+ cards in that suit
2♠ The "default" rebid: 5+ spades and nothing else to show. Any strength
2NT Balanced (e.g. 5-3-3-2) with the unbid suits stopped. Strength not stated yet: 12–14 or 18–19. Balanced without a stopper: rebid 2♠
3♣ 4+ clubs, a real fit for responder
3♠ (jump) Very good 6+ spades, e.g. AKQ1074. Sets spades as trumps
Jump to game Not used here: describe first, decide later

Opener with a minimum doesn't need to rush. Even with 12 points, rebid naturally. You can show "minimum" later by going straight to game (fast arrival).

Responder's second bid

Now responder describes more. After 1♠–2♣–2♦:

Responder bids Meaning
2♠ 3-card spade support. Slow, so it leaves room for slam
4♠ 3-card spade support, minimum: fast arrival, no slam interest
2♥ 4 hearts, or a heart stopper question. Forcing
2NT Balanced, stopper in hearts. Forcing
3NT Balanced minimum, stoppers. No slam interest
3♣ 6+ clubs
3♦ 4-card diamond support

Fast arrival: how strength is shown

Once game is forced, jumping straight to game is the weakest bid. It says "I have nothing extra; stop here". Bidding slowly, below game, says "I have something extra; let's keep exploring".

Auction Meaning
1♠–2♥–4♥ Opener: heart support, minimum. Responder usually passes
1♠–2♥–3♥ Opener: heart support, extra values. Slam is possible
1♠–2♣–2♦–4♠ Responder: spade support, minimum
1♠–2♣–2♦–2♠ Responder: spade support, room to explore slam

This is the reverse of what new players expect: the jump is weak, the slow bid is strong. It works because game is already guaranteed, so slow bidding can't get you dropped too low.

Which game?

Game Points needed When
4♥ / 4♠ About 25 (less with a good fit and shape) First choice with an 8-card major fit
3NT About 25 No major fit, all suits stopped
5♣ / 5♦ About 28–29 Only when 3NT and 4M both look wrong (a suit unstopped, no major fit)
Slam About 33+ Both hands have extras: use slow bidding, control bids, RKCB

24 points is the floor. With a minimum opposite a minimum, 3NT or 4M sometimes goes down one. That's accepted, because the system finds many more games and slams than it loses.

Worked auctions

1. Two minimums: find the fit, stop in game

Opener Responder
♠AQ1074 ♥K83 ♦Q5 ♣J62 (12) ♠K85 ♥A4 ♦J73 ♣KQ1074 (13)
Bid By Meaning
1♠ Opener 5+ spades
2♣ Responder 2/1: 12+, 5 clubs. Game is now forced
2♠ Opener Default rebid: 5 spades, nothing else to show
4♠ Responder 3-card support, minimum: fast arrival
Pass Opener Minimum too. 25 points, 8 spades: a normal game

2. No major fit: 3NT

Opener Responder
♠KQ863 ♥A72 ♦K4 ♣Q93 (14) ♠4 ♥KJ5 ♦AQ1083 ♣KJ74 (14)
Bid By Meaning
1♠ Opener 5+ spades
2♦ Responder 2/1: 12+, 5 diamonds
2NT Opener Balanced
3NT Responder No spade fit, hearts and clubs stopped, no slam interest
Pass Opener 28 points, all suits stopped

3. Both have extras: slow bidding finds the slam

Opener Responder
♠AKJ74 ♥K5 ♦AJ3 ♣Q62 (18) ♠Q85 ♥A4 ♦KQ6 ♣AJ1074 (16)
Bid By Meaning
1♠ Opener 5+ spades
2♣ Responder 2/1, game forcing
2NT Opener Balanced (strength not stated yet)
3♠ Responder 3-card support, bid slowly: "I have extras"
4NT Opener With 18 opposite extras, slam is likely: RKCB
5♠ Responder 2 key cards + the ♠Q
6♠ Opener All 5 key cards and the queen are held. 34 points

If responder had jumped to 4♠ at their second bid (minimum), opener with 18 would still have tried, but responder's slow 3♠ makes the slam easy to bid.

When 2/1 is off

Situation A new 2-level suit means
Responder already passed Natural, 5+ cards, about 10–11, non-forcing. Exception: P–1M–2♣ = Drury
The opponents overcall Natural, 5+ cards, 10+, forcing one round only
The opponents double Natural, 5+ cards, weak, non-forcing
Over 1♣ 1♣–2♦ is a weak jump shift, not a 2/1

A passed hand can't force to game: it has already told partner it doesn't have an opening hand.

If the opponents bid during a 2/1 auction

Game is still forced. You have one extra option: a penalty double of the opponents can replace bidding game, when defending will score more.

Common beginner mistakes

Mistake Correct
Bidding 2♣ with 10–11 "to show the clubs" 2/1 needs 12+. With 10–11, bid 1NT (forcing) and show your hand next time
Passing below game after a 2/1 Never. Even with a bare minimum, keep bidding to game
Jumping to show a good hand Not needed. Bid slowly; the jump to game shows the weak hand
1♠–2♥ with only 4 hearts 2♥ promises 5. With 4 hearts, bid a minor first
Treating 1♥–1♠ as game forcing A 1-level response is only forcing for one round
Making a 2/1 as a passed hand and expecting partner to keep bidding Passed-hand 2-level bids are non-forcing (and 2♣ is Drury)
Forgetting 2/1 is off after an overcall In competition, a new suit is forcing one round only

Forcing 1NT response Tier 0

What it is

1♥–1NT and 1♠–1NT show 6–12 HCP and are forcing for one round: opener must bid again. It is the home for every hand that is too weak for a 2/1 game force and doesn't fit any other response.

It is not forcing if responder is a passed hand or the opponents have interfered.

Hands that respond 1NT

The auction runs: opener 1♠ → responder 1NT (responder's 1st bid) → opener rebids (forced) → responder's 2nd bid. The 2nd bid is where responder shows which kind of 1NT hand it was.

Responder's hand Responder's 1st bid Responder's 2nd bid (after opener's rebid)
Weak balanced (6–10), no fit 1NT Pass, or simple preference to opener's major
Long suit, weak (6–9) 1NT Bid the long suit: 6+ cards, non-forcing
3-card support, 10–12 1NT Jump to 3M (3-card limit raise)
Invitational balanced, 11–12 1NT 2NT
Invitational long suit, 10–12 1NT Jump in the suit (6+ cards)
Over 1♥: 4+ spades 1♠, not 1NT —

Full example: 1♠–1NT–2♣–3♠. Opener opens 1♠; responder bids 1NT; opener rebids 2♣ (forced to bid something); responder now jumps to 3♠, which reveals the 3-card limit raise.

Opener's rebid after 1M–1NT

Opener's hand Rebid
Balanced minimum (5-3-3-2), 12–14 2 of the cheaper 3-card minor. With 3-3 in the minors, 2♣. So 2♣ may be only 3 cards
4+ cards in a lower suit Bid it at the 2-level (1♠–1NT–2♥ = 4+ hearts)
6+ card suit, minimum 2M
6+ good suit, 16–18 3M (invitational)
Balanced 18–19 2NT
Higher new suit (1♥–1NT–2♠) Reverse: 16+, 4 spades, 5+ hearts
19+ with a second suit Jump shift: game forcing

Responder's second bid

  • Pass with a fit for opener's second suit and a minimum.
  • 2M (preference) with 2-card support. You'd have raised directly with 3-card support and 6–9.
  • New suit at the 2-level: 6+ cards, weak, to play.
  • 2NT: 11–12 balanced, invitational.
  • 3M: 3-card limit raise.
  • Raise opener's second suit: 10–12 with 5+ support, invitational.

Examples

  • ♠4 ♥KQ9853 ♦862 ♣Q74 (7 HCP). Partner opens 1♠. Respond 1NT; over opener's 2♣ or 2♦, bid 2♥ (weak, long hearts).
  • ♠K74 ♥A83 ♦Q962 ♣J52 (10 HCP, 3 spades). Partner opens 1♠. Respond 1NT, then jump to 3♠ next (3-card limit raise).
  • Opener holds ♠AQ853 ♥K4 ♦Q74 ♣J62 (12). After 1♠–1NT, rebid 2♣: the cheaper 3-card minor.

Raising partner's major Tier 0

The raise ladder

Response to 1♥ / 1♠ Trumps Strength (dummy points)
2M 3+ 6–9
1NT, then 3M Exactly 3 10–12 (limit raise)
3M 4+ 10–12 (limit raise)
2NT (Jacoby) 4+ 13+ (with 10+ HCP), game forcing
Splinter (double jump in a new suit) 4+ 10–14 HCP, singleton or void in the bid suit
4M 5+ Weak, distributional (preemptive)

Edges. With 4 trumps and 13+ dummy points but fewer than 10 HCP, make the limit raise: too few high cards for Jacoby. A passed hand never uses Jacoby or a splinter: every raise of 10+ goes through Drury 2♣.

Raise with support before showing a new suit when weak. Over 1♥ with 3 hearts, 4 spades and 7 points, raise to 2♥. The fit is what matters.

Examples:

  • ♠84 ♥K93 ♦QJ74 ♣9862: 6 HCP + 1 for the doubleton = 7. Over 1♥, bid 2♥.
  • ♠K5 ♥Q1083 ♦A764 ♣852: 9 HCP + 1 = 10, 4 trumps. Over 1♥, bid 3♥ (limit raise).

Jacoby 2NT

What it is: 1♥–2NT or 1♠–2NT shows 4+ trumps and game values (13+ dummy points, 10+ HCP). It sets trumps and forces to game. Opener then describes the hand:

Opener rebids Meaning
3 of a new suit Singleton or void in that suit
4 of a new suit Good 5-card side suit (two of the top three honors)
3M 18+, no shortness (slam interest)
3NT 15–17, no shortness
4M Minimum (12–14), no shortness. Responder usually passes

Responder then: with a minimum and wasted values opposite opener's shortness (for example KQx opposite a singleton), sign off in 4M. With extras or well-placed values, make a control bid or use RKCB.

Example: Responder ♠K1074 ♥A5 ♦KQ83 ♣J62 (13) bids 2NT over 1♠. Opener ♠AQ853 ♥KQ2 ♦J1074 ♣5 has a singleton club, so rebids 3♣. Responder's ♣J is wasted, so they sign off in 4♠.

Splinter bids

What it is: a double jump in a new suit shows:

  • 4+ card support for partner,
  • a singleton or void in the suit you bid,
  • game values: about 10–14 HCP. Stronger hands start with Jacoby 2NT instead.
After 1♥ After 1♠
3♠, 4♣, 4♦ 4♣, 4♦ (4♥ is natural, to play)

Purpose: opener can now judge slam by how well the hands fit. Honors opposite partner's shortness (KQx facing a singleton) are wasted. Aces and honors in the other suits are gold.

  • Opener with wasted values in the short suit → sign off in 4M.
  • Opener with no waste and extras → control bid or RKCB.

Don't splinter with a singleton ace or king: partner will count that honor as wasted.

Example: ♠KQ5 ♥Q1074 ♦A9863 ♣4 (11 HCP). Over 1♥, bid 4♣. If partner holds ♣xxx, slam is likely; if partner holds ♣KQx, they'll stop in 4♥.

Opener can splinter too. After a 1-level response, opener's double jump in a new suit or jump reverse shows 4-card support, shortness in that suit and about 18+ points: 1♣–1♥–3♠, 1♦–1♠–4♣, 1♦–1♠–3♥.

Over a minor opening, responder's double jump in a major is a splinter for opener's minor (5+ support, game forcing, no 4-card major): 1♦–3♠.

Game tries after 1M–2M

With about 15–17 points, opener can invite game:

  • New suit = help-suit game try. "I need help in this suit." Bid a side suit with two or three losers (e.g. K653).
  • Responder accepts (bids 4M) with help in that suit: A, K, Q, a singleton or a doubleton. Responder also accepts with a maximum raise.
  • Responder declines (bids 3M) with three or more small cards in it and a minimum.
  • 3M = general invite. Responder accepts with a maximum.
  • 4M = to play.

Example: Opener ♠AKJ74 ♥A6 ♦K653 ♣82 (15). After 1♠–2♠, bid 3♦. Responder holding ♦Q4 accepts; holding ♦972 declines.

Responding to 1♣ / 1♦ Tier 0

Showing a major

  • 4-4 in the majors: bid 1♥ first (cheaper suit, "up the line"). Opener will show spades if they have them.
  • 5-4 or longer: bid the longer major first. With 5-5, bid 1♠.
  • Over 1♣, skip diamonds (Walsh): with a 4-card major and fewer than 12 HCP, show the major even if your diamonds are longer. Bid 1♦ first only with game-forcing values (12+), or when you have no 4-card major.

Walsh example: ♠KJ74 ♥83 ♦Q9752 ♣K6 (9). Over 1♣, respond 1♠. If you bid 1♦, the opponents could raise hearts before you ever show spades.

Consequence: a 1♠ response over a minor denies 4 hearts, unless responder has 5+ spades (and so bid the longer suit first).

Other responses

Response Meaning
1NT 6–10, balanced, no 4-card major
2NT 11–12 balanced, no 4-card major, invitational
3NT 13–15 balanced, no 4-card major
4♥ / 4♠ (proposed) 7+ cards in the major, to play, little interest in slam. With slam interest bid 1M first (forcing) and jump to game later if partner does not help
1♦–2♣ 2/1 game forcing, 12+, usually 5+ clubs
2m (raise) Inverted minor: 10+, forcing (Tier 1)
3m (raise) Weak, preemptive: 5–9, 5+ card support
Single jump in a new suit (1♣–2♦, 1♦–2♥, 1♣–2♠) Weak jump shift: 6+ cards, 2–5 HCP
Double jump in a major (1♦–3♠) Splinter for opener's minor

Example: ♠K73 ♥Q82 ♦A94 ♣Q1063 (11). Over 1♣, respond 2NT.

Weak jump shifts

1♦–2♥: 6+ hearts, about 2–5 HCP. "My suit will play better than your 1♦." Opener usually passes. Weak jump shifts also apply in competition.

Why weak? In 2/1, a strong responder just bids a new suit (forcing), so a jump isn't needed for strength. Using it for weak hands gets bad hands with a long suit out of 1NT or 1♦.

Opener's rebids Tier 0

After a 1-level response

Rebid Meaning
1NT 12–14 balanced
New suit at the 1-level Natural, 4+, 12–18 (e.g. 1♣–1♥–1♠ = 4 spades). Not forcing, but responder passes only with about 0–7 and support; with 8–10 bid 1NT or a weak raise
Rebid own suit at the 2-level 6+ cards, minimum (12–15)
New lower suit at the 2-level (1♥–1♠–2♣) Natural, 4+, 12–18. Not a reverse
Raise responder's major to 2 4 trumps (occasionally 3 with a ruffing value), 12–15
Jump raise to 3 4 trumps, 16–18
Raise to 4 4 trumps, 19–20
2NT (jump) 18–19 balanced
Jump rebid of own suit 6+ good cards, 16–18, invitational
Reverse 16+, see below
Jump shift (1♦–1♠–3♣) 19+, game forcing
Double jump / jump reverse Splinter (see Splinter bids)

After 1m–1M–1NT or any three 1-level bids, responder continues with XYZ (Tier 1).

Reverses Tier 0

What a reverse is

Opener's second bid is a new suit at the 2-level that ranks higher than the first suit.

Auction Reverse? Why
1♦–1♠–2♥ Yes Hearts outrank diamonds
1♣–1♥–2♦ Yes Diamonds outrank clubs
1♣–1♠–2♥ Yes Hearts outrank clubs
1♥–1NT–2♠ Yes Spades outrank hearts
1♥–1♠–2♣ No Clubs are lower
1♦–1♠–3♣ No That's a jump shift

Why it shows strength: in 1♦–1♠–2♥, if responder prefers diamonds they must go to 3♦. Opener has pushed the auction a level higher, so opener must have a good hand.

The preference test

To check whether your second suit is a reverse, ask: "If partner likes my first suit better, at what level do they have to say so?"

Auction Partner's preference bid Result
1♦–1♠–2♣ 2♦ (still the 2-level) Normal rebid, 12–18
1♦–1♠–2♥ 3♦ (forced up to the 3-level) Reverse: needs 16+
1♣–1♠–2♦ 3♣ Reverse: needs 16+
1♥–2♣–2♠ 3♥ Game is already forced, so the extra level is safe: shape only

With a minimum opener (12) and a weak responder (6), the side has only about 18 points. That's too few to be safe at the 3-level, so opener only forces partner up there with 16+. After a 2/1, both hands have 12+ and game is guaranteed, so the extra level costs nothing and no extra strength is needed.

What it promises

  • 16+ points, no upper limit.
  • First suit longer than the second (5-4, 6-4, 6-5). With equal lengths you never reverse.
  • Forcing for one round.

When the suits are the same length

Hand Opening Why no reverse is ever needed
5-5 The higher suit The second suit is lower
4-4 minors 1♦ That's why 1♣ then 2♦ promises longer clubs
4♥ + 4♦, unbalanced 1♦ (1♥ needs 5) Rebid notrump or raise partner instead
4-4, balanced 15–17 1NT No rebid needed

With 4♥ 4♦ after 1♦–1♠: rebid 1NT with 12–14 or 2NT with 18–19, or raise spades with 4. If responder has hearts too (5♠ + 4♥), they'll show them next through XYZ.

Too weak to reverse? Don't

♠5 ♥AQ74 ♦KJ953 ♣K82 (13). After 1♦–1♠ you can't bid 2♥. Rebid 1NT; a singleton in partner's suit is acceptable here. Hiding the hearts is better than lying about your strength.

A real reverse: ♠5 ♥AQ74 ♦AKJ83 ♣K62 (17). After 1♦–1♠, bid 2♥.

Responder after a reverse (Lebensohl 2NT)

After 1♦–1♠–2♥:

Responder bids Meaning
2NT Weak (about 5–7). Opener must bid 3♣; responder then passes, or signs off (3♦ = to play in diamonds, 3♥ = to play in hearts with 4)
2♠ (rebid own suit) 5+ spades, forcing one round
3♦ (preference) Game forcing, diamond support
3♥ (raise) Game forcing, 4 hearts
3♣ (4th suit) Game forcing, asks opener to describe further
3NT Natural, to play, stopper in the unbid suit

Opener bids something other than 3♣ over the 2NT relay only with a very strong hand (18+). That bid is natural and forcing to game.

After a 2/1 game-forcing response (1♦–2♣–2♥), the "reverse" just shows shape. Game is already forced, so it promises no extra points.

Responder can reverse too: 1♣–1♥–1NT–2♠ is game forcing. Most of these auctions go through XYZ's 2♦ instead.

1NT opening and responses Tier 0

The response table

After 1NT (15–17) Meaning
Pass 0–7, balanced
2♣ Stayman: asks for a 4-card major
2♦ Transfer: 5+ hearts
2♥ Transfer: 5+ spades
2♠ Minor puppet: forces 3♣ (weak hand with a long minor)
2NT 8–9 balanced, invitational
3♣ / 3♦ Good 6-card minor (2 of the top 3 honors), invites 3NT
3♥ / 3♠ 3♠ = both minors, slam interest (proposed); 3♥ not used
3NT 10–15, to play
4♣ Gerber: asks for aces
4♦ / 4♥ Texas: transfer to 4♥ / 4♠, to play
4NT 16–17 balanced, quantitative: invites 6NT

Stayman (2♣)

Opener replies: 2♦ = no 4-card major · 2♥ = 4 hearts (may also have 4 spades) · 2♠ = 4 spades, not 4 hearts.

Responder continues:

Auction Meaning
1NT–2♣–2♦–2♥ / 2♠ 5 cards in the bid major + 4 in the other, invitational
1NT–2♣–2♦–3♥ / 3♠ Smolen: 4 in the bid major + 5 in the other, GF (Tier 2)
1NT–2♣–2♦–2NT 8–9, invitational, a 4-card major but no fit
1NT–2♣–2♥–2♠ 4 spades (not 4 hearts), invitational
1NT–2♣–2♥–3♥ 4 hearts, invitational
1NT–2♣–2♥–3NT 4 spades, game values. Opener with 4 spades corrects to 4♠
Raise to game in a fit To play

Opener after 1NT–2♣–2♥–2NT or –2♠: if opener also has 4 spades, they bid spades (at 3♠ with a minimum, 4♠ with a maximum after an invite).

Garbage Stayman. With a weak hand and 4-4 in the majors plus long diamonds (short clubs), bid 2♣ and pass whatever opener replies. All three replies are safer than 1NT.

Example: ♠J863 ♥Q752 ♦97632 ♣— (3 HCP). Bid 2♣, then pass 2♦, 2♥ or 2♠.

Game example: ♠KJ63 ♥Q1074 ♦K52 ♣Q4 (11). Bid 2♣. Over 2♦ bid 3NT; over 2♥ bid 4♥; over 2♠ bid 4♠.

Jacoby transfers (2♦ / 2♥)

2♦ asks opener to bid 2♥; 2♥ asks opener to bid 2♠. The strong hand becomes declarer, so the opening lead comes up to it.

Opener's reply:

  • Normally accept: bid the next suit.
  • Super-accept with 4-card support and a maximum (17): jump to 3M.

Responder's second bid after the transfer (e.g. 1NT–2♥–2♠):

Next bid Meaning
Pass Weak (0–7), 5+ spades
2NT Exactly 5 spades, invitational (8–9)
3♠ 6+ spades, invitational
3NT Exactly 5 spades, game values: choose 3NT or 4♠
4♠ 6+ spades, game, mild slam interest (use Texas to just sign off)
New suit at the 3-level Natural, 4+ cards, game forcing
4NT Quantitative with 5 spades (not RKCB)

5-5 in the majors:

  • Weak → transfer to spades, pass.
  • Invitational → 2♦, then 2♠.
  • Game forcing → 2♥, then 3♥.

Example: ♠KQ1063 ♥84 ♦J72 ♣853 (6). Bid 2♥, then pass 2♠.

Minor puppet (2♠)

1NT–2♠ forces opener to bid 3♣. Responder then:

  • passes with long clubs, or
  • bids 3♦ to play in diamonds.

Both are weak hands. Example: ♠4 ♥J82 ♦Q987632 ♣73: 2♠, then 3♦.

Invitational 3♣ / 3♦

1NT–3♦ shows a good 6-card suit (AQJ953, KQ10xxx) and invites 3NT: "if you can stop the other suits and have a fitting honor, my suit will run". Opener bids 3NT or passes.

Example: ♠84 ♥73 ♦AQJ953 ♣842: bid 3♦.

Texas transfers (4♦ / 4♥)

1NT–4♥ asks opener to bid 4♠ (and 4♦ asks for 4♥). Use Texas with a 6+ card major and game values but no slam interest: it signs off, with the strong hand as declarer.

Example: ♠KQJ8743 ♥5 ♦K62 ♣84: bid 4♥, then pass 4♠.

Texas vs Jacoby with a 6-card major:

Sequence Meaning
1NT–4♥–4♠–pass Sign-off
1NT–2♥–2♠–4♠ Mild slam interest
1NT–4♥–4♠–4NT RKCB for spades
1NT–2♥–2♠–4NT Quantitative with 5 spades

Gerber (4♣)

4♣ directly over partner's 1NT or 2NT (including 2♣–2♦–2NT) asks for aces:

Reply Aces
4♦ 0 or 4
4♥ 1
4♠ 2
4NT 3

After the reply, 5♣ asks for kings with the same steps. Any notrump bid by the asker is to play.

Gerber only applies directly over notrump. Everywhere else, 4♣ is natural or a splinter.

Quantitative 4NT

1NT–4NT = 16–17 balanced, no interest in a suit. Opener passes with 15, bids 6NT with 17, and judges with 16 (a good 5-card suit or tens and nines: bid on).

When they interfere over our 1NT

Their action Our method
Double Systems on: Stayman and transfers as usual. XX = we have the balance of strength, about 9+
Artificial overcall (the bid doesn't show the suit named, e.g. 2♣ = both majors) Stolen bid: X means what their bid would have meant for us (X of 2♣ = Stayman, X of 2♦ = transfer to hearts). Everything else systems on
Natural 2-level overcall Lebensohl (Tier 2)

2NT opening (20–21)

Same structure, one level higher:

After 2NT Meaning
3♣ Stayman (Smolen applies after 3♦)
3♦ / 3♥ Transfer to ♥ / ♠
3♠ Both minors (5-4 or longer), slam interest
3NT To play
4♣ Gerber
4♦ / 4♥ Texas
4NT Quantitative

Gambling 3NT

Opening 3NT shows a solid 7+ card minor (AKQxxxx or longer) and no ace or king outside. Partner:

  • passes with stoppers in the other suits,
  • bids 4♣ (pass-or-correct: opener passes with clubs, bids 4♦ with diamonds) to run,
  • bids 5♣ pass-or-correct to play game in the minor.

Weak twos and Ogust Tier 0

Opening a weak two

  • 6-card suit, 5–10 HCP.
  • 2♦, 2♥ and 2♠ are all weak.
  • In 1st and 2nd seat: no 4-card side major and no void. Keep the suit decent (two honors).
  • In 3rd seat you can be lighter or use a good 5-card suit. In 4th seat there's no reason to preempt: open normally or pass.

Example: ♠KQJ953 ♥74 ♦K82 ♣63 (9). Open 2♠.

Responses

Response Meaning
Raise (2♠–3♠) Preemptive, to play. Not invitational
4M To play: either expecting to make, or a bigger preempt
New suit Natural, 5+ cards, forcing one round
2NT Ogust: asks about strength and suit quality
3NT To play

Ogust replies

Reply Strength Suit quality
3♣ Minimum (5–7) Bad
3♦ Minimum (5–7) Good
3♥ Maximum (8–10) Bad
3♠ Maximum (8–10) Good
3NT Solid suit (AKQxxx)

Good suit = 2 of the top 3 honors (AK, AQ, KQ).

Memory hook: minor replies = minimum, major replies = maximum. Within each pair, the lower bid is the bad suit.

Example: Partner opens 2♠ holding ♠KQJ953 ♥74 ♦K82 ♣63 and you ask with 2NT holding ♠A4 ♥AK63 ♦A975 ♣Q82. Partner replies 3♠ (maximum, good suit): bid 4♠. Over 3♣ (minimum, bad suit) you'd stop in 3♠.

Preempts Tier 0

  • 3-level opening: about 7 cards, weak (less than an opening hand). Not vulnerable you can be braver.
  • 4-level opening: about 8 cards.
  • Responses: a new suit is forcing. A raise is to play. 3NT over a minor preempt is to play.
  • In 3rd seat be more aggressive; in 4th seat don't preempt.

Competitive bidding Tier 0

Overcalls

Overcall Requirements
1-level suit 5+ cards, 8–16 HCP
2-level suit Good 5+ cards (usually 6), 11–16
Jump overcall, e.g. (1♣)–2♥, or (1♠)–3♥ Weak, 5–10. Landing at the 2-level, 6 cards, like a weak two. Landing at the 3-level (e.g. (1♠)–3♥), 7 cards, like a weak three. A good suit (two of the top three honors) in both cases
1NT (direct) 15–18 balanced with a stopper in their suit. Systems on (Stayman, transfers)
1NT in 4th seat (balancing) 11–14 balanced
Cue-bid of their suit Michaels
Jump to 2NT Unusual 2NT
Double Takeout

Advancing partner's overcall

Advancer bids Meaning
New suit Natural, 5+ cards, non-forcing
Simple raise 6–9, 3+ support. A raise to the 3-level (e.g. of a 2-level overcall) needs 4 trumps and 6+, or 3 trumps and 8+ (one more when vulnerable)
Jump raise Preemptive: weak with 4+ support
Cue-bid of their suit 10+ with support: limit raise or better
1NT 8–11 with a stopper
2NT 11–12 with a stopper

Example: (1♣)–1♥–(P)–? holding ♠K84 ♥Q963 ♦AJ2 ♣854 (10 HCP, 4 hearts). Bid 2♣: a good heart raise. With ♠K84 ♥Q963 ♦972 ♣854 (5 HCP), just raise to 2♥.

Takeout doubles

Requirements: shortness in their suit (ideally 0–2 cards), support for the unbid suits, about 12+ HCP. Any 17+ hand also starts with a double and bids again.

Advancing after (1♥)–X–(P):

Advancer bids Meaning
Cheapest suit 0–8
Jump in a suit 9–11, invitational
Cue-bid of their suit 12+, forcing
1NT 6–10 with a stopper
2NT 11–12 with a stopper
3NT 13+ with a stopper
Pass Penalty: strong long trumps in their suit (rare)

If RHO bids after the double, advancer is no longer forced; bidding shows about 6+.

Doubler bids again voluntarily = 17+ (a new suit shows a strong one-suited hand).

After a balancing double (1x)–P–(P)–X–(P): advancer must still bid (pass only with long, strong trumps). Partner may be light, so jump only with 11–12, bid notrump with 10–12 and a stopper, and cue-bid with 13+.

Later in the auction too: whenever partner's double is for takeout (see the general rule below) and the next player passes, you must bid: your best unbid suit (a 4-card major first), notrump with a stopper, or game with 12–13+. Pass only to defend: 5+ trumps, or 4 with an honor when they are at the 3-level. A pass is not "no opinion": it turns partner's double into a penalty double.

Michaels cue-bid

A cue-bid of the opener's suit at the 2-level shows a 5-5 two-suiter (5-4 not vulnerable at your discretion):

Auction Shows
(1♣)–2♣ or (1♦)–2♦ Both majors
(1♥)–2♥ Spades + a minor
(1♠)–2♠ Hearts + a minor

Strength: either weak (6–11) or very strong (16+), never in between. With a middle hand, overcall the higher suit and bid the other later.

Advancer bids the preferred suit at the cheapest level (jump = invitational). After a major-suit Michaels, 2NT asks for the minor.

Unusual 2NT

A jump overcall of 2NT shows 5-5 in the two lowest unbid suits:

Over 2NT shows
1♥ or 1♠ Clubs + diamonds
1♣ Diamonds + hearts
1♦ Clubs + hearts

Strength as for Michaels.

Negative doubles (through 3♠)

When partner opens and RHO overcalls a suit (up to 3♠), a double is for takeout and focuses on the unbid major(s).

Auction Double shows
1♣–(1♦)–X Both majors, at least 4-4 (bid 1♥/1♠ with only one major)
1♣–(1♥)–X Exactly 4 spades (1♠ would show 5+)
1♦–(1♠)–X 4+ hearts, 6+ HCP (2♥ would show 5+ hearts and 10+)
1♥–(1♠)–X Both minors, or a hand with no good bid
1♦–(2♣)–X Both majors, or one major without the strength to bid it at the 2-level
1♥–(2♦)–X 4 spades + clubs, or a hand without a good bid

Minimum strength: 6+ at the 1-level, 8+ at the 2-level, 10+ at the 3-level.

Free bids in competition:

  • New suit at the 1-level: 4+ cards (but 1♠ after a 1♥ overcall promises 5+), forcing.
  • New suit at the 2-level: 5+ cards, 10+, forcing one round.
  • With a penalty double of their overcall in mind: pass. Opener, short in their suit, reopens with a double, and you pass for penalty.

Opener after a negative double: bid the shown major at the cheapest level with a minimum and 4 cards, jump with 15–17, cue-bid their suit with a big hand, or pass for penalty with a trump stack.

When they overcall our opening

Responder bids Meaning
Simple raise 6–9
Jump raise Preemptive, 4+ trumps, weak
Cue-bid of their suit Limit raise or better in opener's suit (10+)
Negative double See above
New suit Forcing one round
1NT Natural, about 8–10 with a stopper in their suit
Single jump in a new suit Weak jump shift (as without competition)

Example: 1♥–(2♣)–? holding ♠A73 ♥K962 ♦QJ4 ♣652 (10 HCP): bid 3♣ (good heart raise). With ♠73 ♥K9862 ♦Q84 ♣652 (5 HCP), bid 3♥ (preemptive).

Inverted minors and 2/1 are off after an overcall: 1♦–(1♠)–2♦ is a normal weak raise, and the strong raise goes through the cue-bid 2♠.

When they double our opening

After 1♠–(X):

Responder bids Meaning
XX 10+ HCP, usually no fit (plans to double them or show a suit)
New suit at the 1-level Natural, forcing
New suit at the 2-level Natural, 5+ cards, weak, non-forcing
2♠ Weak raise, 6–9
2NT (Jordan) 4+ trumps, limit raise or better (Tier 1)
3♠ Preemptive, 4+ trumps, weak

Against their weak twos and preempts

Auction Meaning
(2♥)–X Takeout: opening values, short in hearts
(2♥)–2NT 15–18 balanced with a heart stopper
(2♥)–2♠ / 3♣ / 3♦ Natural, good 5+ suit, about 12+
(2♥)–3♥ Asks partner for a heart stopper (for 3NT with a long running minor)
(3♠)–X Takeout
(3♠)–3NT To play

Advancing a double of a weak two (Lebensohl): after (2♥)–X–(P):

  • 2NT = weak (0–7). Forces 3♣; advancer passes or signs off in a suit.
  • Direct 3-level suit bid = 8–11, constructive.
  • Cue-bid (3♥) = game forcing, asks for a 4-card spade suit or a stopper.
  • Game bid = to play.

Penalty or takeout? The general rule

Double is TAKEOUT when... Double is PENALTY when...
Low-level suit bid, and we haven't found a fit yet We've already agreed a fit
It's a negative, responsive, support or Lebensohl situation They bid notrump
They bid a game freely (not a sacrifice)
Partner's previous double already showed values (e.g. after a redouble)

Defense: leads and signals Tier 0

Opening leads against a suit contract

Holding Lead
A-K-x Ace
K-Q-x, Q-J-10, J-10-9 (any sequence) Top card
Long suit with an honor (K-J-6-3) 4th best (the 3)
Doubleton (8-4) Top card (the 8)
Three small (9-6-2) Top card (the 9)
Singleton Good choice if partner may have an entry to give you a ruff
A-x-x (no king) Never underlead at trick 1: lead the ace or another suit

Opening leads against notrump

Holding Lead
Long suit with an honor (K-J-7-5-2) 4th best (the 5)
Solid or broken sequence: K-Q-J, K-Q-10, Q-J-9 Top card
Interior sequence: K-J-10, Q-10-9, A-J-10 Top of the inner sequence (J, 10, J)
Four small (8-6-4-2) Second highest (the 6): "I have nothing here"
Partner bid a suit Usually lead partner's suit

Signals (Standard)

Situation Signal
Partner leads a suit, you follow Attitude: high = "continue", low = "switch"
Declarer leads a suit Count: high-low = even number, low-high = odd
Partner leads a likely singleton / the switch is obvious Suit preference: high card = the higher remaining suit, low = the lower
Your first discard Attitude: high = "I like this suit"

Habits that save tricks

  • Second hand low, third hand high.
  • Cover an honor with an honor when it can promote a card for your side.
  • Count declarer's tricks and the points shown in the bidding; partner's count signal tells you how many cards declarer has.
  • Return partner's suit against notrump unless you have a clearly better plan.

Inverted minor raises Tier 1

What it is

The meaning of a minor-suit raise is "inverted" from the old style: the simple raise is strong and the jump raise is weak.

Auction Meaning
1♣–2♣ / 1♦–2♦ 10+ HCP, forcing one round. 5+ clubs or 4+ diamonds. No 4-card major
1♣–3♣ / 1♦–3♦ Weak, preemptive: 5–9 HCP, 5+ card support

Opener's rebid after 1m–2m

Opener bids Meaning
2NT 12–14 balanced. Non-forcing
3NT 18–19 balanced
New suit at the 2-level Stopper in that suit, natural, forcing. Heading for 3NT
3m Minimum, unbalanced. Non-forcing
Jump in a new suit Splinter: shortness, slam interest

Responder then: with 10–12, may pass 2NT or 3m. With 13+, keep going to game.

When it's off

In competition (after an overcall or a double), 1m–2m goes back to a normal weak raise (6–9). The strong raise goes through the cue-bid of their suit, or Jordan 2NT after a double.

Example

Responder ♠K4 ♥A73 ♦KJ1052 ♣Q62 (13, no 4-card major). Over 1♦, bid 2♦. Opener ♠AQ6 ♥KJ4 ♦Q874 ♣953 (12, balanced) bids 2NT. Responder, with 13, bids 3NT.

Traps

  • Don't use 2m with a 4-card major. Show the major first.
  • If the opponents bid, the old meaning returns: 2m is weak.

XYZ Tier 1

When it applies

Whenever the first three bids are all at the 1-level, or opener rebids 1NT:

  • 1♣–1♥–1♠
  • 1♦–1♠–1NT
  • 1♣–1♦–1♥

It replaces New Minor Forcing and checkback. It's off in competition.

Responder's next bid

Responder bids Meaning
2♣ Relay: opener must bid 2♦. Responder then passes (weak with diamonds) or makes an invitational bid
2♦ Artificial, game forcing
2 of a new lower-ranking suit (e.g. 1♦–1♠–1NT–2♥) Weak, natural, to play (5♠ + 4♥)
2 of own suit (e.g. 1♦–1♠–1NT–2♠) Weak, 6+ cards, to play
2NT Puppet to 3♣, to play in clubs (or 3♦ after it)
Jump to 3 of a suit Game forcing, good 6+ suit
3NT / 4M To play

After the 2♣ relay (invitational hands)

1♦–1♠–1NT–2♣–2♦–?

Responder bids Meaning
Pass Weak with diamonds
2♥ 5♠ + 4♥, invitational
2♠ 6+ spades, invitational
2NT Balanced, invitational (opener can bid 3♠/4♠ with 3-card support)
3♦ Diamond support, invitational

Opener accepts with a maximum (13–14) and declines with a minimum.

After the 2♦ game force

Opener describes the hand in this order of priority:

  1. 3-card support for responder's major: bid 2 of it.
  2. An unbid 4-card major: bid it.
  3. Stopper in the unbid suit: 2NT.
  4. Otherwise rebid your long suit.

Examples

  • ♠Q8743 ♥K952 ♦4 ♣J73 (6). 1♦–1♠–1NT–? Bid 2♥: weak with 5♠ + 4♥. Opener passes or corrects to 2♠.
  • ♠AJ743 ♥K952 ♦4 ♣Q73 (10). 1♦–1♠–1NT–? Bid 2♣, then over 2♦ bid 2♥: invitational, 5♠ + 4♥.
  • ♠AQ74 ♥K6 ♦J5 ♣KJ1063 (14). 1♦–1♠–1NT–? Bid 2♦: game forcing. You'll find out whether spades or notrump is right.

Traps

  • Over 2♣, opener has no choice: bid 2♦.
  • XYZ is only for three 1-level bids (or a 1NT rebid). After 1♦–1♠–2♣ use fourth suit forcing instead.

Fourth suit forcing Tier 1

What it is

When three suits have been bid by our side, responder bidding the fourth suit at the 2-level or higher is artificial and game forcing. It says: "I have game values but don't know where to play. Tell me more."

1♦–1♠–2♣–2♥: 2♥ is fourth suit forcing. It does not promise hearts.

(At the 1-level, e.g. 1♣–1♦–1♥–1♠, the fourth suit is natural; XYZ covers those auctions.)

Opener's reply, in order of priority

  1. 3-card support for responder's first suit: raise it.
  2. Stopper in the fourth suit: bid notrump (2NT; minimum or maximum is clarified later).
  3. Extra length in a suit already bid: rebid it.
  4. 4 cards in the fourth suit: raise it.

Example

Responder ♠AQ753 ♥843 ♦K5 ♣A62 (13). 1♦–1♠–2♣–? There's no heart stopper for 3NT and no fit yet, so bid 2♥. If opener bids 2NT (heart stopper), raise to 3NT. If opener bids 2♠ (3-card support), bid 4♠.

Drury Tier 1

What it is

A passed-hand responder's 2♣ over partner's 1♥/1♠ shows 3+ card support and 10–11 points (a limit raise). It lets opener stop at the 2-level after a light 3rd- or 4th-seat opening.

P–1♠–2♣ = Drury (not clubs).

Opener's rebid

Opener bids Meaning
2M Light opening, no game interest. Responder passes
4M Full opening, to play
Any other bid Full opening values, natural game try

When it applies

  • On when RHO passes, and on after a double (P–1♠–(X)–2♣). Over the double, Jordan 2NT shows the 4-card limit raise and 2♣ the 3-card one.
  • Off after an overcall: use the cue-bid raise instead.

Example

You passed, partner opened 1♠ in 3rd seat. You hold ♠KJ5 ♥Q842 ♦A73 ♣965 (10). Bid 2♣. Partner, with a light ♠AQ1074 ♥K3 ♦862 ♣J74 (10), signs off in 2♠.

Jordan 2NT Tier 1

What it is

After partner's opening and RHO's takeout double, 2NT shows a limit raise or better with 4+ card support (5+ for a minor).

Responder bids after 1♥–(X) Meaning
2♥ Weak raise, 6–9
2NT 4+ trumps, 10+
3♥ Preemptive: 4+ trumps, weak
XX, then raise 3-card limit raise

Opener: 3♥ = minimum, stop · 4♥ = accept game · new suit = slam interest.

Example

♠84 ♥KJ73 ♦A962 ♣Q53 (10). 1♥–(X)–? Bid 2NT.

DONT against their 1NT Tier 1

What it is

DONT ("Disturb Opponents' No Trump") gets into the auction cheaply against an opponent's 1NT opening, mostly with two-suited hands. We use it against every 1NT, strong or weak, in direct and balancing seat.

Our call over (1NT) Shows
X One long suit (6+). Partner bids 2♣; you pass with clubs or bid your suit
2♣ Clubs + a higher suit (5-4 or longer)
2♦ Diamonds + a major
2♥ Hearts + spades
2♠ Spades only (6+ usually)

Strength: a good playing hand, roughly 8–15 HCP. A balanced 15+ hand just passes and defends.

Advancing (partner's DONT bid)

After partner's Advancer
X Bids 2♣ (forced, unless you have a long suit of your own to play)
2♣ Pass with clubs support, or 2♦ = "show me your other suit"
2♦ Pass with diamonds, or 2♥ = pass-or-correct (pass with hearts, partner bids 2♠ with spades)
2♥ Pass with hearts, or 2♠ with spades
2♠ Pass, or raise with a fit

In general: with support for the suit shown, pass. Otherwise bid the next step up to find the second suit.

Examples

  • ♠KQ1074 ♥AJ863 ♦5 ♣84: over (1NT), bid 2♥ (both majors).
  • ♠4 ♥KQJ1073 ♦A84 ♣953: X. Over partner's 2♣, bid 2♥.
  • ♠KQ84 ♥5 ♦63 ♣AJ10862: 2♣ (clubs + a higher suit).

RKCB 1430 and slam tools Tier 1

Roman Key Card Blackwood (4NT)

There are five key cards: the four aces and the king of trumps. 4NT asks how many partner holds:

Reply Key cards
5♣ 1 or 4
5♦ 0 or 3
5♥ 2, without the trump queen
5♠ 2, with the trump queen

Memory hook: "1430" = the 5♣ reply is 1 or 4, the 5♦ reply is 0 or 3. The bidding context always tells you which.

When 4NT is RKCB

  • A suit has been agreed (directly, or through Jacoby 2NT, a splinter or Texas). The trump suit is the agreed suit.
  • If no suit is agreed, the last suit bid naturally is trump.
  • After notrump bidding with no agreed suit (e.g. 1NT–4NT), 4NT is quantitative, not RKCB.

Follow-ups

  • Queen ask: after a 5♣ or 5♦ reply, the next step that isn't the trump suit asks for the trump queen. Responder with no queen bids the trump suit at the cheapest level; with the queen, bids anything else (6 of the trump suit is simplest).
  • 5NT asks for kings and promises all five key cards and the trump queen. Replies by number, not counting the trump king: 6♣ = 0, 6♦ = 1, 6♥ = 2, 6♠ = 3.
  • Sign-off: 5 of the trump suit.
  • Decide: missing 2 key cards → stop at the 5-level. Missing 1 → small slam. Missing none plus the queen → think about a grand slam.

When they interfere

They... Our replies
Overcall 4NT X = 0 or 3 · Pass = 1 or 4 · next step = 2 without Q · second step = 2 with Q
Double 4NT XX = 0 or 3 · Pass = 1 or 4 · next step = 2 without Q · second step = 2 with Q

Voids

We don't show voids in RKCB replies. Count only your key cards. With a void and slam interest, use control bids instead of Blackwood.

Control bids (cue-bids)

Once a suit is agreed and game is forced, bidding a new suit at the 4-level (or 3-level) shows a first- or second-round control there: ace, king, void or singleton.

  • Bid the cheapest control first, going up the line.
  • Skipping a suit denies a control in it.
  • Returning to 4 of the trump suit = no extra interest.

Use control bids instead of RKCB when you have a void, or when two quick losers in one suit could beat the slam.

Example

1♥–2NT (Jacoby) –3♣ (club shortness) –4NT (RKCB, hearts) –5♠ (2 key cards + ♥Q) –6♥.

Support doubles and redoubles Tier 2

What it is

After 1m–(P)–1M (or 1♥–1♠), if RHO interferes at a level up to 2 of responder's suit:

Opener's call Meaning
X (after an overcall) Exactly 3-card support for responder's major
XX (after a double) Exactly 3-card support
Raise 4-card support
Other bids Natural, denying 3-card support

It shows the length of support only. It promises no extra strength.

Limit: on through 2 of responder's suit (2♥ when responder bid hearts, 2♠ for spades).

Example

1♦–(P)–1♥–(1♠)–? Opener holds ♠84 ♥K73 ♦AQ953 ♣K62 (12). Bid X (exactly 3 hearts). With 4 hearts, bid 2♥.

What responder does next

Responder treats the support double like a raise: with a 5-card suit, you know of an 8-card fit. With a 4-card suit, the fit is only 7 cards, so look elsewhere or play notrump.

Trap

Opener can't make a penalty double of the overcall. With a trump stack in their suit, pass and hope partner reopens with a double.

Smolen Tier 2

What it is

After 1NT–2♣–2♦ (no 4-card major), responder with 5-4 in the majors and game values jumps in the 4-card major:

Responder bids Shows
3♥ 4 hearts + 5 spades, game forcing
3♠ 4 spades + 5 hearts, game forcing

Opener: with 3-card support for the 5-card major, bid game in it (4♠ after 3♥, 4♥ after 3♠). Otherwise bid 3NT.

Why: the strong 1NT hand ends up as declarer in the major fit.

Example

♠KQ1063 ♥A984 ♦85 ♣Q4 (11). 1NT–2♣–2♦–? Bid 3♥. Opener with ♠J72 bids 4♠; with ♠72 bids 3NT.

Related bids

  • Weak 5-4: transfer to the 5-card major and pass.
  • Invitational 5-4: 1NT–2♣–2♦–2♥/2♠ (5 cards in the bid major).
  • 6-4: transfer to the 6-card major and bid game (Texas with no slam interest).

Lebensohl Tier 2

What it is

Lebensohl uses 2NT as a relay to 3♣ so you can sign off cheaply at the 3-level, while direct 3-level bids show strength. We use the same relay in three places.

1. After our 1NT and a natural 2-level overcall

1NT–(2♥)–?

Responder bids Meaning
2♠ Natural, 5+ spades, to play (competitive)
2NT Relay: opener must bid 3♣
…then pass To play in clubs
…then 3♦ (a suit below theirs) To play
…then 3♠ (a suit above theirs) Invitational, 5+ spades
Direct 3♣ / 3♦ / 3♠ Game forcing, 5+ cards
Direct 3♥ (cue-bid) Stayman for spades, no heart stopper
2NT, then 3♥ Stayman for spades, with a heart stopper
Direct 3NT To play, no heart stopper
2NT, then 3NT To play, with a heart stopper
X Penalty

Memory hook: "Fast denies, slow shows." Going straight to 3NT or the cue-bid denies a stopper. Going through 2NT first shows one.

2. After a reverse

1♦–1♠–2♥–2NT: responder is weak and forces 3♣, then passes or signs off. See Reverses.

3. After partner doubles their weak two

(2♥)–X–(P)–2NT: advancer is weak (0–7) and forces 3♣, then passes or signs off. A direct 3-level bid shows 8–11. See Against their weak twos and preempts.

Trap

The 2NT relay is forcing. The opener (or doubler) must bid 3♣ even with a good hand, except after a reverse with 18+.

Strong 2♣ opening Tier 2

Opening 2♣

22+ balanced, or an unbalanced hand with about 9 playing tricks and a strong suit. Artificial: says nothing about clubs.

Responses

Response Meaning
2♦ Waiting: any hand without a positive. Says nothing about diamonds
2♥ / 2♠ / 3♣ / 3♦ Positive: good 5+ suit (2 of the top 3 honors), 8+ HCP
2NT Positive: 8+ balanced, no good suit

Opener's rebid after 2♣–2♦

Rebid Meaning
2NT 22–24 balanced. Systems on (3♣ Stayman, transfers, Smolen, Gerber, Texas)
3NT 25–27 balanced. Systems on
2♥ / 2♠ / 3♣ / 3♦ Natural, 5+ cards, game forcing (unless responder makes a second negative)

Second negative

After 2♣–2♦–2♥ (or 2♠), 3♣ = second negative: 0–3 HCP, "I have nothing". If opener rebid 3♣, the second negative is 3♦; over 3♦ it is 3♥. After a second negative, opener's rebid of the suit can be passed.

Game forcing?

After 2♣, the auction is forcing to game, except:

  • after the 2NT rebid (22–24), which responder may pass with 0–2;
  • after a second negative.

If they interfere over 2♣

Pass = weak (0–3) · X = some values (4+) · a bid = natural positive.

Example

♠AKQ1073 ♥AK4 ♦A5 ♣K2 (23 HCP, about 10 tricks). Open 2♣. After 2♦, bid 2♠ (game forcing).

New agreements (proposed, Oct 2026) Tier 1

Proposed — confirm with partner. These fill gaps the system did not cover. They are the most common standard treatments.

Lead-directing doubles

A double of an artificial bid asks partner to lead that suit. It shows a good suit (two of the top three honors, usually 5 cards), not values.

Their auctionOur double means
(1NT)–P–(2♣)–XLead clubs (doubling their Stayman)
(1NT)–P–(2♦)–X, (1NT)–P–(2♥)–XLead the suit doubled (their transfer)
(2NT)–P–(3♣ / 3♦ / 3♥)–XSame, one level higher
(4NT)–P–(5x)–XLead the suit of their key-card reply

Against their strong 2♣

Over (2♣), or over (2♣)–P–(2♦)Meaning
XLead-directing: a good club suit (over 2♦: a good diamond suit)
Suit bidNatural, 5+ cards (usually 6), preemptive: take their room
Jump in a suit7+ cards, preemptive
2NT5-5 in the minors, preemptive
PassAnything else

Responsive doubles

Partner doubled for takeout or overcalled, and they raise their suit (to 2 or 3). Our double is responsive: about 8+ points and the unbid suits, no clear suit to bid.

  • (1♦)–X–(2♦)–X = both majors, 8+.
  • (1♣)–1♥–(2♣)–X = spades and diamonds (the unbid suits), 8+, not enough ♥ support to raise.
  • With support for partner's overcall, raise instead. With one long suit, bid it.

Competing at the 3-level

  • Law of Total Tricks: compete to the level of your combined trumps − 6 (8 trumps → 2-level, 9 → 3-level). With a game hand, bid game anyway.
  • Maximal double: when we have agreed a suit and they bid the suit just below ours at the 3-level, a double is our only game try. 1♥–(2♦)–2♥–(3♦)–X = game try; 3♥ = competing only.
  • When they bid any other suit at the 3-level, a double is for penalty.

Vulnerability

VulnerabilityPreempts and weak jump overcallsCompeting
We are vulnerableSound: 7+ HCP and two of the top three honorsTo the Law of Total Tricks level, no further
Neither / bothNormal: 5–10 HCP, two honorsLaw of Total Tricks
Favorable (they are, we are not)Can be light: 4+ HCPOne level higher than the Law (a cheap sacrifice)

1♥/1♠–3NT

15–17 balanced with exactly 2 cards in opener's major (no 4-card side major). Game forcing; opener chooses: pass with a balanced minimum, 4M with 6+ cards or an unbalanced hand, 4NT (quantitative) with 16–17, 6NT with 18+.

Passed-hand jump shifts

After we have passed, a jump shift over partner's 1♥/1♠ is fit-showing: a good 5-card suit (two of the top three honors) and 4+ card support, about 10–11. P–1♥–3♦ = good diamonds and 4 hearts. Weak jump shifts are off for a passed hand (with a weak long suit, bid 1NT or pass).

RKCB when a minor is trumps

4NT can take us too high in a minor (a 5♥ or 5♠ reply is already past 5♣/5♦). Use 4NT in a minor only with 2+ key cards of your own; otherwise bid 5 of the minor, or 6 with clear extra values.

When they show two suits over our opening

Over their Michaels cue-bid or Unusual 2NT: cue-bid of the cheaper of their known suits = limit raise or better in our suit; a raise of our suit is competitive; double = values (10+), usually short in our suit, looking to penalize them; new suits are natural.

  • 1♥–(2♥)–2♠: they showed spades (+ a minor) → 2♠ = good heart raise.
  • 1♣–(2NT)–3♦: they showed ♦ + ♥ → 3♦ = good club raise.

Two-suiters over their weak two (Leaping Michaels)

Our cue-bid of their weak two asks for a stopper, so two-suited hands jump to the 4-level instead. 5-5 or longer, game values (about 11+ HCP with that shape).

  • (2♥)–4♣ / 4♦ = that minor + spades. (2♠)–4♣ / 4♦ = that minor + hearts.
  • (2♦)–4♦ = both majors; (2♦)–4♣ = clubs + a major.

Doubling their 4-level preempts

  • Over 4♣ / 4♦ / 4♥: X = takeout (short in their suit, 13+). Over 4♥, partner bids 4♠ with 4 spades, or passes with trump tricks.
  • Over 4♠: X = values (14+); partner usually passes, pulling only with a long suit and a singleton spade. 4NT = takeout for two suits (5-5).
  • A new suit at the 5-level is natural: a good 6+ card suit.

Strong minor hands over our 1NT

  • 1NT–3♠ = both minors (5-4 or longer), slam interest. Opener: 3NT = no 4-card minor; 4♣/4♦ = a fit, slam is possible.
  • 1NT–2♠–3♣–4♣ / 4♦ = a strong 6+ card minor, slam try. Opener: 6 of the minor with 16–17 and 3+ cards, otherwise 5.
  • Weak minor hands still use 2♠ and pass or bid 3♦.

Doubling their slam (Lightner)

A double of a slam they bid freely is not for trump tricks: it asks partner for an unusual lead — not our suit; usually dummy's first-bid suit — typically because the doubler is void and can ruff, or has an AK in that suit.

Opener after 1♥/1♠–1NT and their overcall

Their overcall ends the forcing 1NT: opener no longer has to bid. Responder (6–12) still gets another turn.

Opener bidsMeaning
PassMinimum, nothing more to show (the most common call)
2M6+ cards, minimum (3M when 2M is no longer available: 7+ cards, or 6 and extra values)
Jump to 3M6+ cards, 16–18: invitational
XTakeout: short in their suit with extra values (13+ with a singleton, 16+ with a doubleton), or any 18+. Responder passes with length in their suit
New suitNatural, 5+ cards, not forcing (at the 3-level: 5-5 or 15+)
2NT / 3NT18–19 / 20–21 balanced with a stopper in their suit

Example: 1♠–P–1NT–(2♦) holding ♠AKQ85 ♥J7 ♦Q84 ♣Q105 (14): pass. Minimum, balanced, no sixth spade, and no shortness in diamonds. With ♠AKQ85 ♥KJ7 ♦4 ♣KQ105 (17), double.

After opener's double: responder passes for penalty with 5+ cards in their suit (or 4 good ones), bids notrump with a stopper, gives preference to opener's major with 2 cards, or bids a 4+ suit. With 10+, jump.

Opener's reopening double

After 1x–(overcall)–P–(P), partner may have passed with a penalty double in mind (we play negative doubles). So opener, short in their suit, reopens with a double.

Opener bidsMeaning
X0–1 cards in their suit with any opening; 2 cards unless opener has a 6-card suit to rebid; or any 19+
Rebid own suit6+ cards (jump with 16–18)
New suit5-5 or 6-5, natural
Notrump18–19 balanced with a stopper
Pass3+ cards in their suit and nothing to add

Responder: pass for penalty with 5+ trumps (or 4 good ones); otherwise bid as if answering a takeout double. With 10+, jump or bid 3NT with a stopper.

When they double after partner's pass (1♦–P–P–(X)): partner is weak, so there is no game. Rebid a 6-card suit (competing, not extra strength); with 5-4 and 13+, show the second suit (4+, not forcing; a reverse still needs 16+); otherwise pass and compete later if needed. Redouble = 18+, suggesting we can penalize them.

Support doubles after their overcall

Support doubles also apply when the left-hand opponent overcalled first and responder bid a major at the 1-level. 1♦–(1♥)–1♠–(2♥)–X = exactly 3 spades. As before, the limit is 2 of responder's suit.

Opener's other bids, here and in the usual support-double auctions, are natural and deny 3-card support:

  • A raise = 4+ cards (jump raise 16–18).
  • A new suit = 4+ cards (5-5 at the 3-level; a 2-level suit above opener's first suit is a reverse: 16+).
  • 1NT = 12–14; 2NT = 18–19 (both need stoppers).
  • A cue-bid of their suit = 18+ without a clear bid, forcing.
  • Pass = no support and nothing more to say.

Opener after a negative double when they raise

1♣–(1♦)–X–(3♦): their raise takes away opener's normal reply. Opener still shows the major partner promised:

  • A 4-card major partner showed: bid it (game with 16+).
  • 17+ with a stopper in their suit: 3NT.
  • Any other 17+: double (cooperative: partner passes with their suit, or bids).
  • 6+ cards in opener's suit: rebid it.
  • Otherwise: pass (minimum).

Advancing when they bid over partner's overcall

After (1x)–overcall–(their new suit, 1NT or a negative double), advance as without their bid, one step higher if needed:

  • A raise = 3+ cards, 6–9; a jump raise = 4+ cards, weak (preemptive). A raise that has to go to the 3-level needs real values: 4-card support with 6–9, or 3-card support with 8–9 (9 when vulnerable). Otherwise pass: their new suit is forcing, so you get another chance.
  • A cue-bid of opener's suit = 10+ with 3+ support.
  • Notrump = stoppers in their suits (1NT 8–11, 2NT 11–12, 3NT 13+).
  • A new suit = 5+ cards, not forcing.
  • After their negative double, XX = 10+, usually without a fit.

Do not raise on a bad hand just because of the fit. A raise promises 6+ points, unless you have 9+ trumps between you.

Danger zones: the most common mistakes

Mistake The rule
Treating every 4♣ as Gerber 4♣ is Gerber only directly over partner's 1NT or 2NT (including 2♣–2♦–2NT). Anywhere else it's natural or a splinter
Treating every 4NT as Blackwood 4NT is RKCB only when a suit is agreed. After notrump bidding with no agreed suit, it's quantitative
Reversing with a minimum A reverse needs 16+ and a longer first suit. Otherwise rebid 1NT or your suit
Expecting extras from a reverse after 2/1 After a 2/1 response, a "reverse" shows shape only
Looking for 4 hearts after 1m–1♠ 1♠ over a minor denies 4 hearts unless spades are 5+
Playing inverted minors or 2/1 in competition Both are off after an overcall or double
Treating P–1♠–2♣ as a game force A passed hand can't force to game; it's Drury
Passing a forcing 1NT 1M–1NT is forcing: opener must bid again (unless responder passed earlier)
Bidding on after a 2♣ relay in XYZ Opener must bid 2♦
Forgetting the Lebensohl relay is forcing After 2NT, partner must bid 3♣
